newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end brutal week with solid gain.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end brutal week with solid gain.

text.p: U.S. stocks ended with solid gains on Friday, capping a week that saw shares suffer the fourth-largest point loss in New York Stock Exchange history.
Inspired by a second-day rally in high-technology shares, the Dow industrials rose 49 points, or 0.75 percent, to 6526.
While market players expressed relief the blood-letting on Wall Street had abated, many said stocks were not ready to race back yet.
"I'd rather sell on strength than buy on dips here," said James Volk, director of equity trading at Jensen Securities.
For the week, the blue chip gauge lost more than 214 points, putting it behind the 216-point loss suffered the week ended October 13, 1989 on the list of biggest NYSE weekly losses.

However, on a percentage basis the week's losses were not among the NYSE's largest. The three percent drop during the week paled against the 13 percent drop registered during the week of the October 1987 Black Monday crash.
Stocks rallied despite renewed weakness in the bond market following a nervously awaited report on U.S. March employment.

Although non-farm payroll growth slowed to a smaller-than- expected 175,000 non-farm jobs last month from 293,000 in February, the unemployment rate crept down to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent and wages crept upward.
Concerns that a tight labor market might bring further Federal Reserve interest rates sent the 30-year Treasury bond down 21/32 to yield 7.12 percent in late trading.
But equity investors appeared ready for some bargain hunting, particularily in high technology stocks.
The Nasdaq composite finished up 23 points, or 1.9 percent, at 1237. It rose 13 points on Thursday.
Before Thursday's session the Nasdaq index had fallen 13.5 percent off its January 22 record high closing level.

Leading the way were semiconductor stocks, with Intel Corp up 4-3/8 to 145 and Applied Materials Inc up 3-3/4 to 52-1/4. Among other rebounding high-tech shares was Dow industrial component Hewlett-Packard Co, which rose 2-1/8 to 52-3/4.

Market watchers said stocks could be finding a near-term low, with the Dow bouncing off the 6400 level. "If the bonds will behave, I think the market could go back up for a while," said Bruce Bittles, market strategist at J.C. Bradford.
But the rebound on Friday may not mean the sell-off on Wall Street has run its course.

"You can have substantial rallies and still not be out of the woods yet," said Jonathan Dodd, technical analyst at Dean Witter. Staples Inc rose 5/8 to 21-7/8 and Office Depot Inc sank 5-5/8 to 13-3/8 after the Federal Trade Commission voted to reject their proposed merger. Office Depot Chairman David Puente called the decision "absurd."
International Business Machines Corp gave up 1-7/8 to 129-1/4. Merrill Lynch cut its near-term rating on the stock to neutral from buy.

Checkpoint Systems Inc lost 2-5/8 to 10-1/8 and Ultrak Inc fell 4-5/8 to 11-7/8 after the two makers of security systems canceled a $397 million merger agreement and projected lower-than-expected first quarter earnings.
Transport stocks rallied and oil shares slipped as world oil prices sank to new nine-months lows in a market weakened by concerns about crude oversupply.

The Dow Jones transport index .DJT jumped two percent. Among its components was American Airlines' parent AMR Corp, which shot up 3-7/8 to 86-3/8, also boosted by a vote by the board of its pilots union to approve a labor contract.
